lines: A graph where every vertex can reach every other looks, from a distance, exactly like one where only small pockets can reach each other.
Telling the two apart, even on a graph with a billion edges, takes exactly one more depth-first search.
Just one extra number carried alongside each vertex.
Take any directed graph, find every one of these mutually-reachable groups, and shrink each one down to a single point.
Is what's left always acyclic, sometimes acyclic, or never acyclic?
answer: If those shrunken points still formed a cycle, it would mean their original groups could all reach each other — forward and back. But then they weren't separate groups to begin with. They'd already have been one.

lines: Here's the first way to find these groups: one single pass of depth-first search.

Alongside the usual discovery order, carry one more number for each vertex — the smallest discovery number reachable from it, through the search tree and through edges back up to something still active.
The instant that number catches back up to the vertex's own discovery number, pop everything above it off the stack. That's a complete group, found on the spot.
Here's a second way, simpler to describe: run depth-first search once, just to get a finishing order.
Reverse every edge in the graph.

Run depth-first search again, in that reversed finishing order — and every new tree this second pass builds is exactly one of these groups. Simpler to picture, but it costs a second full pass and a reversed copy of the graph, against the first method's single pass.
Shrink every one of those groups down to a point, on this same graph.
What's left has no cycle in it — not by assumption, but checked directly, with the exact same cycle test built earlier in this chapter.
A cycle among the shrunken points would mean they were never really separate to begin with.
Now take a hard-looking logic problem instead: a formula built from pairs of either-or clauses, and the question of whether any assignment of true and false can satisfy every one of them.
Turn each clause into a pair of implications, and look at the resulting graph's own groups.
If some variable and its own opposite end up in the same group, is that formula satisfiable, unsatisfiable, or does it depend on everything else in the formula?
answer: Unsatisfiable. Always, no matter what else is in the formula.

Landing in the same group means each one forces the other to carry the same value. But a variable and its own opposite can never share a value — one is true exactly when the other is false. No assignment can get around that.

lines: One key, one boundary, one order statistic — that was the last chapter's whole business.
This chapter asked something different about a graph with no weights anywhere: what can reach what, and which groups can all reach each other.
Every single answer cost exactly one pass over the graph. The next question puts a cost on every edge, and asks for the cheapest way through.
